image.altEn: Spanish-language xkcd comic: one person challenges another for judging people who photograph a sunset.

titleText.es: Odio que la gente le haga fotos a la comida en lugar de comérsela, porque no hay nada que me guste más que el sonido de la gente masticando.
titleText.en: I hate when people take photos of their meal instead of eating it, because there's nothing I love more than the sound of other people chewing.

regions.labelEs: UF, ODIO QUE LA GENTE HAGA FOTOS EN LUGAR DE DISFRUTAR DE LA VISTA. ¿POR QUÉ?
regions.translationEn: Ugh, I hate that people take photos instead of enjoying the view. Why?
regions.noteEn: Odiar que reacts to another person's action and takes the subjunctive haga.

applications.explanationEn: Odio gives the emotional reaction. Que introduces what other people do, so hacer appears in the subjunctive form haga.
Here en lugar de introduces the action chosen as the alternative.
Here disfrutar de connects the act of enjoying to what is being enjoyed.
Here hacer una foto means taking a photo; le and the words after a can identify what is photographed.
Qué keeps its accent inside por qué because the phrase asks “why.”
This is the two-word question form por qué, meaning “why.” The one-word answer form porque means “because.”
Here de is required by the verb before the following complement. Translate the complete verb pattern, not de by itself.

regions.labelEs: DOCUMENTAR TU VIDA TE DISTRAE DE VIVIRLA. EN REALIDAD, NO… VENGA YA.
regions.translationEn: Documenting your life distracts you from living it. Actually, no… Oh, come on.
regions.noteEn: The final la in vivirla refers back to vida. Venga ya rejects the claim impatiently.

applications.explanationEn: Here en realidad signals a correction or qualification of the preceding idea.
Here venga ya is a fixed reaction showing disbelief or impatience, not a literal request to come.

regions.labelEs: SI INTENTO HACERLE UNA FOTO A ALGO, LE VOY A PRESTAR MÁS ATENCIÓN. ALGUNAS DE MIS MAYORES AVENTURAS HAN SURGIDO AL INTENTAR FOTOGRAFIAR ALGO.
regions.translationEn: If I try to take a photo of something, I'll pay more attention to it. Some of my greatest adventures have come from trying to photograph something.
regions.noteEn: Le refers to the subject of the photo; ir a plus an infinitive expresses the expected result.

applications.explanationEn: Here prestar atención works as one expression meaning “to pay attention”; prestar is not being used as “to lend.”
Here hacer una foto means taking a photo; le and the words after a can identify what is photographed.
Voy shows who acts, a links the verbs, and prestar stays in its unchanged dictionary form. Together they mark the following action as planned or expected.
Al plus the infinitive intentar marks when the adventures arose: “when trying.”
Han is the they form of haber, followed by surgido. The adventures happened before now but are being discussed as part of the speaker's experience.
Here le points back to algo—the thing that will receive the speaker’s attention.

regions.labelEs: SI TE MOLESTA QUE OTRA GENTE TENGA EXPERIENCIAS DE FORMA ‘INCORRECTA’, IMAGINA QUÉ INSOPORTABLE ES QUE UN DESCONOCIDO CONDESCENDIENTE TE DIGA QUE ODIA LA FORMA EN QUE VIVES TU VIDA JUSTO EN EL MOMENTO EN QUE HAS ENCONTRADO ALGO QUE QUIERES RECORDAR. ¿POR QUÉ COÑO TE IMPORTA CÓMO DISFRUTAN OTROS DE UNA PUESTA DE SOL?
regions.translationEn: If it bothers you that other people have experiences the ‘wrong’ way, imagine how unbearable it is to have a condescending stranger tell you they hate the way you live your life just when you've found something you want to remember. Why the fuck do you care how other people enjoy a sunset?
regions.noteEn: Coño is deliberately vulgar, strengthening an angry challenge to the stranger's judgment.

applications.explanationEn: Molesta gives the reaction. Que introduces another group's action, so tener appears in the subjunctive form tenga.
Es insoportable gives the judgment. Que introduces the action being judged, so decir appears in the subjunctive form diga.
Has is the tú form of haber, followed by encontrado. The thing was found earlier and is still important at this moment.
Te names the person affected (“to you”), while the situation is what matters. In natural English, the question asks why you care.

applications.exampleEs: DISFRUTAN OTROS DE UNA PUESTA DE SOL
applications.explanationEn: Here disfrutar de connects the act of enjoying to what is being enjoyed.
Here puesta de sol works as one noun expression meaning “sunset.”
Qué carries an accent here because it is exclamative: qué insoportable means “how unbearable.”
Qué keeps its accent inside por qué because the phrase asks “why.”
Cómo carries an accent because it introduces the embedded question of how other people enjoy the sunset.
This is the two-word question form por qué, meaning “why.” The one-word answer form porque means “because.”
Here te marks “you” as the person affected by the verb rather than as its subject.
Here qué intensifies insoportable. The combination means “how unbearable,” not “what unbearable.”
Here te marks “you” as the person affected by the verb rather than as its subject.
Here que connects the noun before it to a description of that noun.
Here que connects the noun before it to a description of that noun.
Here que connects the noun before it to a description of that noun.
Here te marks “you” as the person affected by the verb rather than as its subject.

regions.labelEs: BUENO, PORQUE… PORQUE YO SOLO, EH… CLIC
regions.translationEn: Well, because… because I just, uh… Click.
regions.noteEn: Unable to justify his complaint, the critic becomes the subject of the other person's photo.

applications.explanationEn: Here bueno opens a hesitant response and gives the speaker time; it does not describe something as good.

cards.answerEn: Use he, has, ha, hemos, habéis, or han followed by the verb’s completed-action form.
cards.noteEn: These are forms of haber, the helper verb used here like English “have.” For most verbs, the completed-action form ends in -ado after an -ar verb and -ido after an -er or -ir verb. This form is called the past participle, and it does not change after haber. How often this tense is used instead of the simple past varies by region.
cards.questionEn: How do you say “have done,” as in “I have finished”?

example.en: I have finished.

cards.answerEn: Spanish puts that second verb in a special form called the subjunctive.
cards.noteEn: The first part expresses someone’s feeling or reaction. Que means “that” and introduces what they are reacting to. When the part after que has its own doer, Spanish normally changes its verb to the subjunctive: estás becomes estés in the example. English does not need a separate word for this change.
cards.questionEn: What happens to the second verb after phrases such as “I’m glad that…” or “It bothers me that…”?

example.en: I am glad that you are here.

cards.promptEs: es + adjetivo de valoración + que + subjuntivo
cards.answerEn: Use the subjunctive for the situation being judged.
cards.noteEn: Phrases such as es importante, es bueno, and es raro express a judgment about what follows. Spanish marks the verb after que with the subjunctive. In the example, descansas—the ordinary statement form—changes to descanses.
cards.questionEn: After “It is important/good/strange that…,” which form does the next Spanish verb take?

example.en: It is important that you rest.

cards.answerEn: Write qué, cómo, cuándo, and similar words with an accent when they ask a question or add an exclamation.
cards.noteEn: This includes direct questions (¿Qué quieres?), questions inside another sentence (No sé qué quiere), and exclamations (¡Qué bonito!). Without the accent, these words usually connect parts of a sentence instead: el libro que quiero means “the book that I want.”
cards.questionEn: Why do words such as que, como, and cuando sometimes have a written accent?

example.en: What is your name?

cards.noteEn: Write the question form as two words, with an accent on qué. Write the usual answer word porque as one word without an accent.
cards.questionEn: How do you write “why” and “because” in Spanish?

example.es: ¿Por qué estudias español? Porque me gusta.
example.en: Why do you study Spanish? Because I like it.

cards.noteEn: After en lugar de, use a thing or the dictionary form of an action verb. That dictionary form is called the infinitive and usually ends in -ar, -er, or -ir.
cards.questionEn: How do you say “instead of” before a thing or an action?

example.en: We walk instead of driving.

cards.answerEn: Disfrutar de followed by a thing means “to enjoy that thing.”
cards.noteEn: De introduces what is being enjoyed and usually has no separate English word here. Spanish can also use disfrutar directly without de in many contexts, so learn disfrutar de as a common pattern rather than an unbreakable rule.
cards.questionEn: How does disfrutar de connect “enjoy” to the thing being enjoyed?

example.en: We enjoy the music.

cards.noteEn: Learn these three words as one noun expression. Puesta means “setting” here, so the phrase literally describes the setting of the sun.
cards.questionEn: What is the usual Spanish expression for “sunset”?

example.es: Vimos una puesta de sol preciosa.
example.en: We saw a beautiful sunset.

cards.noteEn: English uses “pay,” but Spanish uses prestar, a verb that by itself often means “to lend.” Add a before the person or thing receiving the attention: prestar atención a algo.
cards.questionEn: How do you say “to pay attention” in Spanish?

example.en: Pay attention to the question.

cards.promptEs: hacer una foto · hacerle una foto a alguien/algo
cards.answerEn: Use hacer una foto; to name what is photographed, use hacerle una foto a alguien or algo.
cards.noteEn: Hacer normally means “to make” or “to do,” but in this expression it corresponds to English “take.” Le and the words after a point to the person or thing in the photo. Tomar una foto is common in many other regions.
cards.questionEn: In Spain, how do you say “to take a photo” or “to take a photo of someone”?

example.es: Vamos a hacerle una foto al perro.
example.en: We are going to take a photo of the dog.

cards.answerEn: Use a form of ir (“to go”), then a, then the action verb in its dictionary form.
cards.noteEn: Ir changes to match the person: voy a means “I am going to,” vas a means “you are going to,” and va a means “he/she is going to.” The final action stays in its unchanged -ar, -er, or -ir form. This pattern expresses a plan, intention, or expected future event.
cards.questionEn: How do you say that someone is going to do something?

example.en: I am going to study.

cards.answerEn: Use al followed by the action verb in its dictionary form.
cards.noteEn: The dictionary form ends in -ar, -er, or -ir and is called the infinitive. Al + verb tells when the main action happens. Translate it naturally as “when,” “on,” or “upon”: al llegar means “when arriving” or simply “when someone arrives.”
cards.questionEn: How do you say “when doing something” or “upon doing something”?

example.en: When I arrive, I will call you.

cards.noteEn: Use it to correct or qualify what someone may believe. It does not mean “currently”; Spanish normally uses actualmente for that meaning.
cards.questionEn: What expression means “actually” or “in fact” when correcting an impression?

example.es: Pensaba que era lunes, pero en realidad es martes.
example.en: I thought it was Monday, but it is actually Tuesday.

cards.answerEn: It means “Oh, come on!” or “No way!”
cards.noteEn: Venga by itself is a form of venir, “to come,” but the complete expression is a fixed reaction. Tone can make it sound playful, disbelieving, or annoyed.
cards.questionEn: In Spain, what does ¡Venga ya! mean when someone reacts with disbelief or impatience?

example.en: —He says he won by himself. —Oh, come on!

cards.answerEn: The thing that matters chooses importa or importan; me, te, le, nos, or les says who cares.
cards.noteEn: Spanish builds this idea from the thing outward. Me importa el libro literally says “The book matters to me,” so the singular el libro uses importa. Me importan los libros says “Books matter to me,” so the plural los libros uses importan. The small word identifies the affected person: me means “to me,” te means “to you,” and le can mean “to him,” “to her,” or formal “to you.”
cards.questionEn: Why does me importa work like “it matters to me” rather than “I care about it”?

example.en: Your opinion matters to me; I care about your opinion.

cards.answerEn: It can mean “well…,” giving the speaker time or softening the reply.
cards.noteEn: Here bueno organizes the conversation rather than describing a person or thing. A pause after it can signal hesitation, reluctance, or a gentle correction.
cards.questionEn: What can bueno mean at the start of an answer when it is not describing something as good?

example.en: Well… I don't know.

cards.answerEn: to (part of ir a + infinitive, going to do something)
of (marks what the photo is of)
no separate English word; a required verb complement
cards.noteEn: Some Spanish verbs require de before their complement or a following infinitive. English often absorbs this de into the verb’s translation: dejar de means “to stop doing,” while disfrutar de means “to enjoy.”

example.en: I stopped smoking.

cards.answerEn: in (as part of de forma, in a … way)
to take a photo of it or them (in hacerle una foto)
cards.noteEn: Hacerle combines hacer with the indirect-object pronoun le. In hacerle una foto a algo or alguien, the full expression means “to take a photo of it or them.”

example.es: Quiero hacerle una foto al edificio.
example.en: I want to take a photo of the building.

cards.noteEn: Here le points back to a thing and functions as an indirect-object pronoun with prestar atención. A fuller a + noun phrase can state what le refers to.

example.es: A esta cuestión le presto mucha atención.
example.en: I pay close attention to this issue.

cards.answerEn: to pay (as part of prestar atención)
cards.noteEn: Prestar normally means “to lend,” but prestar atención is a fixed expression meaning “to pay attention.”

example.en: Pay attention to the explanation.

cards.noteEn: Que connects a noun to information describing it. Depending on the noun, English translates it as “who,” “that,” or “which.”

example.es: La persona que llamó es mi amiga.
example.en: The person who called is my friend.

cards.noteEn: Que introduces a clause after verbs such as creer, saber, esperar, or decir. English often uses “that,” but may leave it unstated.

example.en: I think that Ana is coming.

cards.answerEn: how (to what a degree, as in qué insoportable)
cards.noteEn: Qué before an adjective can express a strong degree, like English “how” in “how strange!” It keeps its written accent.

example.en: How beautiful the garden is!

cards.answerEn: actually; in fact (as part of en realidad)

cards.noteEn: Te can mean “to you” when you are the recipient or the person affected by an action. It normally appears before a conjugated verb.

example.en: I’m sending you a message.

cards.answerEn: adds impatient emphasis in venga ya (come on!)
